Yves Klein - 4th Dan Judoka and Famous Artist

I recall on the old Judo Forum a fellow had started a post on Yves Klein. He was a Judo historian. He wrote up the following on Yves Klein:

It odd that so little is written or discussed these days in judo books or on judo forums about the person of Yves Klein. In my view, Klein was one of the most remarkable Western judoists of all time. When you Google his name together with the term judo, many of the returns have little to do with judo sites, but with art sites.

For those who are not familiar with the name, Yves Klein was a French-Jewish artist. He was one of the first people of name to travel to Japan and get acquainted with Japanese society and study kata in depth. In 1953, at the age of just 25, Klein obtained the rank of Kodokan, 4th dan, a quite remarkable achievement in those days.

He wrote Les fondaments du judo, a book when put in perspective is quite unique for those days. Other judo books existed, but except for, perhaps, Charles Yerkow, not too many Westerners were paying close attention to kata in their book. Klein's 1953 book already contained a close study of such advanced kata like Koshiki-no-kata and Itsutsu-no-kata, with Klein himself participating. In his book, Klein features as uke in Koshiki-no-kata with Asami Sampei as tori, and he also features as uke in Itsutsu-no-kata with Oda Join as tori.

Klein was an artist of name, part of the avant-garde of his time. Among his friends he could count world famous music composers and other artists.

It seems to me that very little about Klein has reached the Anglo-Saxon judo world, and I would be interested to hear from people in this forum, including professional researchers like Joe Svinth, how well they are acquainted with Klein and his work, and why neither they, nor most of the judo world seems to devote considerable attention to him, unlike what they do or have done to people like Feldenkrais or Bonet-Maury ?

Klein's life was somehow also remarkably tragic. He died in 1962 at just 34 years of age. Similarly baffling, is that the relatively new French judo federation in those days ... refused to accept and honor his Kodokan judo grade ! Apparently, this caused Klein deep grief, to the extent that he left the country and went to Spain.

Another tragic feature is, that Klein was a pupil to Abe Ichiro. To some degree, Abe-sensei has remained somewhat in the shadow of his colleague judan, Daigo and Osawa. Yet, Abe did form a number of remarkable judoists as a teacher and coach, particularly in France and Belgium; I am thinking of 4-time European champions and world hopeful Daniel Outelet, European champion Theo Guldemont, superb technician Marcel Clause, and Yves Klein. It is particularly tragic that coincidentally, two among these best students lost their lives very early. Klein died at the age of just 34 yrs of a heart attack; I believe he smoked quite a bit, not uncommon in those days, certainly not among artists. Outelet committed suicide at young age.

Wikipedio has a relatively informative entry about Klein http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yves_Klein, but as usual, judo is tyipcally only mentioned as a fait divers, whereas in reality, a Western 4th dan in 1953, could be truly considered as a judo expert.

To me, Klein's role to judo is far more important than realized or acknowledged. His involvement with kata, is not a coincidence. Kata is art; kata is an artistic expression of judo, but kata has so far received very little study or attention in this context. Originally, in judo, kata was really largely created because Kano's group of student had grown so much that he could no longer teach them all; so kata were created as mnemonic to allow junior teachers to have a schedule of progression of techniques. The early kata are then also performed quite different from today's kata, much, much more loose.

Kata then evolved to become largely a pain in the butt for people wanting to achieve promotion. During recent years, kata has entered a rapid of evolution again in becoming part of judo's competitive area.

That being said, very little attention is given, including in Japanese books or in Kodokan circles, to kata as a form of art and artistic expression. Yet, it is. In my personal view, Klein, the sensitive artist, was one of the first people to regognize this multifunctional unit which kata represents.

Because of all these reasons I'd like to see a thread develop around Yves Klein.

I also point out that Klein worked a lot with Igor Correa, who also became a student and one of the foremost students of Hirano Tokio. Correa was devoted to true judo and created a Judo Federation of his own, which had some very interesting principles.

A link from the wayback machine can be found here if you want to see some of the thread: https://web.archive.org/web/20090417210224/http://judoforum.com/index.php?showtopic=25315

Lets rewind 25 years ago. Picture me - at the height of fitness - doing all my ROTC shit because I'm a white male who can't pay for college.

I used to live in Philly. I actually used to live in university city in the dorms. That was expensive as shit but required for first year students so after I bit the bullet the first year I put out an ad and got some roommates and moved to 36th and spring garden. Some context - ROTC was mostly just working out, and at the time the army had a real bias for long range running. If you could do the running you could rack up enough points to do shit work on the other stuff, so all the ROTC officers has us running all the time. We were skinny as shit and generally malnourished because we're not eating 10,000 calories a day.

My running route took me from 36th and spring garden to the art museum and back again after doing my Rocky impersonation.

This went on for a year or so and three incidents stick out in my mind: The first time, I was pursued by a basketball american on (what probably wasn't) his bike. He pretty much ran me down and said "GIBS ME YOH MONEEE". "Well, I'm a poor starving college student, I don't have any". He tossed my wallet off the bridge while making chimp noises and drove off.

Second time about six months later - a different basketball american youth wearing a hoodie stepped out from the bushes and chimped the same message at me. This time I was smart enough to not carry a wallet while running. He settled for punching me in the face repeatedly. I decided to carry a wallet so my folks could collect my corpse.

Third time a basketball american youth wearing a giant fucking jacket was pursuing me on a bike again. This time I knew how this would go down and had started carrying a knife. I took it out and conspicuously held it at my side while running. He followed me a bit and then didn't give anymore chase.

After getting back to my apartment I finally said fuck it and realized if a gang of gorillas decided to chase me down a knife isn't going to do much so I got on the web and looked up gun shops. This was before gunbroker and armslist so I had to actually go outside. However to date myself, at the time the Sig Sauer P220 was only a $250 gun. It also didn't have that stupid rail on the bottom which looks like it would catch on a holster.

Anyway, $250 was still loot to me 25 years ago on poor college money but at the time my folks were still alive and my father was like LET ME BUY THAT FOR YOU.

The rest is history. I tossed the P220 into a fag-bag along with whatever else I didn't want to carry and never got robbed again. It's one of those stupid things where provided I didn't buy the gun, I'd probably have been raped and stabbed by now but since I did put out the money, everyone left me alone. I suppose it's the universe looking out for the idiots who think robbing folks is cool.

It is really hard to imagine you in all of that story ending up in a fanny pack.

Better to have it and not need it than need it and not have it.

They're actually really practical for exactly that purpose. Yeah I could have gone with an IWB holster or something but frankly guns are heavy. Guns + running = goofy weight distribution. I found I didn't like having one side be heavier than another on a 5 miler and since I wanted a place to store my stuff anyway it worked.
